speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: As with any work arrangement, a four-day work week may work well for some employers and employees but not others.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, let me state that the Labour Movement is heartened to hear about the Government's commitment to continue promoting flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has shown all of us that a variety of flexible work arrangements, once thought impossible, can work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To better understand the impact of a four-day work week, would the Ministry be open to conducting a small-scale trial among some of its employees or perhaps within segments of the Public Service?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This way, we can better understand and study the pros and cons, benefits and challenges.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, how a reduced work week can possibly better facilitate and encourage employees' continual training and upskilling because setting aside one day a week for training and upskilling can be a win for both workers and the companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And with better work-life balance, perhaps, a win also for Singapore, with possibly more babies.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: A four-day work week has worked in some companies, places and jobs, but not others.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, we welcome employers and employees out there, whether in the private or public sector, to try the type of flexible work arrangement that they think best suits their workplace.
